walkthroughs.body_html:
Coordination & Control — a core area of GCSE Biology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Coordination & Control brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Coordination & Control.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Adrenaline binds to receptors on the membrane and activates:
options: DNA directly
Adenylyl cyclase to make cAMP
Ribosomes
Lysosomes

mcqs.q: Which gland is referred to as the master gland?
options: Pancreas
Pituitary
Thyroid
Adrenal

mcqs.q: After pre-mRNA splicing in eukaryotes, which sequences remain in the mature mRNA?
options: The refractory period blocks all signals from reaching the neurone.
Exons remain; introns are removed.
Introns remain because they encode the protein; exons are removed as junk.
Both introns and exons are removed and the cell uses just the cap and tail.

mcqs.q: What is the purpose of the refractory period after an action potential?
options: The refractory period exists because the cell runs out of energy and needs a rest.
It ensures action potentials travel in one direction only and limits the maximum firing frequency.
Both introns and exons are removed and the cell uses just the cap and tail.
The refractory period blocks all signals from reaching the neurone.

mcqs.q: Why are food chains usually limited to about 4 or 5 trophic levels?
options: There aren't enough types of animals to fill more trophic levels.
Only ~10 percent of energy is transferred between trophic levels; eventually too little energy remains to support another level.
Larger animals always eat the next ones up, and there aren't enough giant animals.
Both introns and exons are removed and the cell uses just the cap and tail.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Hormone”?
options: Steroid? No: catecholamine secreted by adrenal medulla; activates fight-or-flight, raising heart rate and blood glucose.
Ductless gland secreting hormones directly into the blood, e.g. pituitary, thyroid, pancreas.
Intracellular molecule (e.g. cAMP) that relays a signal from a hormone-receptor binding to enzymes inside the cell.
Chemical messenger secreted into the bloodstream and acting on target cells with complementary receptors.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Second messenger”?
options: Intracellular molecule (e.g. cAMP) that relays a signal from a hormone-receptor binding to enzymes inside the cell.
Ductless gland secreting hormones directly into the blood, e.g. pituitary, thyroid, pancreas.
Steroid? No: catecholamine secreted by adrenal medulla; activates fight-or-flight, raising heart rate and blood glucose.
Peptide hormone from α cells of pancreas; raises blood glucose by promoting glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Endocrine gland”?
options: Peptide hormone from α cells of pancreas; raises blood glucose by promoting glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
Ductless gland secreting hormones directly into the blood, e.g. pituitary, thyroid, pancreas.
Chemical messenger secreted into the bloodstream and acting on target cells with complementary receptors.
Intracellular molecule (e.g. cAMP) that relays a signal from a hormone-receptor binding to enzymes inside the cell.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Adrenaline”?
options: Ductless gland secreting hormones directly into the blood, e.g. pituitary, thyroid, pancreas.
Steroid? No: catecholamine secreted by adrenal medulla; activates fight-or-flight, raising heart rate and blood glucose.
Intracellular molecule (e.g. cAMP) that relays a signal from a hormone-receptor binding to enzymes inside the cell.
Peptide hormone from α cells of pancreas; raises blood glucose by promoting glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Glucagon”?
options: Peptide hormone from β cells of pancreas; lowers blood glucose by stimulating uptake and glycogenesis.
Peptide hormone from α cells of pancreas; raises blood glucose by promoting glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
Intracellular molecule (e.g. cAMP) that relays a signal from a hormone-receptor binding to enzymes inside the cell.
Chemical messenger secreted into the bloodstream and acting on target cells with complementary receptors.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Insulin”?
options: Intracellular molecule (e.g. cAMP) that relays a signal from a hormone-receptor binding to enzymes inside the cell.
Steroid? No: catecholamine secreted by adrenal medulla; activates fight-or-flight, raising heart rate and blood glucose.
Peptide hormone from β cells of pancreas; lowers blood glucose by stimulating uptake and glycogenesis.
Ductless gland secreting hormones directly into the blood, e.g. pituitary, thyroid, pancreas.

mcqs.q: A person's blood glucose rises after a meal. Which hormone is released, and what is its effect?
options: Insulin, which lowers blood glucose
Glucagon, which lowers blood glucose
Insulin, which raises blood glucose
Adrenaline, which lowers blood glucose

mcqs.q: In a frightening situation the heart rate rises and the body prepares for action. Which gland and hormone are responsible?
options: Adrenal gland releasing adrenaline
Pancreas releasing insulin
Thyroid releasing adrenaline
Pituitary releasing glucagon

mcqs.q: Why is the pituitary gland sometimes called the 'master gland'?
options: It releases hormones that control other glands.
It produces all the body's hormones itself.
It is the largest gland in the body.
It releases hormones only through nerves.

mcqs.q: Blood glucose is kept within narrow limits by insulin and glucagon working in opposite ways. This control is an example of:
options: Negative feedback
Positive feedback
A reflex arc
Active transport

free_texts.q: Type the key term that means: "Ductless gland secreting hormones directly into the blood, e.g. pituitary, thyroid, pancreas."
free_texts.hint: It's one of the six key terms above.

sequence.def: A change, e.g. rising blood glucose, is detected
Gland is triggered to act, e.g. the pancreas
Chemical messenger secreted into the bloodstream
Hormone travels to target organs around the body
Hormone fits specific receptors on target cells
Target cells change activity to restore balance
